newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Slow German growth pushes unemployment up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Slow German growth pushes unemployment up.

text.p: German unemployment rose sharply in September, as economic growth is still too low to boost the jobs market, Labour Office President Bernhard Jagoda said on Tuesday.
The number of jobless rose 39,000 to 3.991 million on a seasonally adjusted basis. The adjusted unemployment rate edged up to 10.4 percent from 10.3 percent, the Bundesbank said.
On an unadjusted basis, the number of jobless fell to 3.848 million from 3.902 million.
"The improvement (in the unadjusted data) was relatively weak due to too-low economic growth," Jagoda said. "We have not yet felt growth impulses from the economy in the jobs market."
"I can't yet see any significant turnaround," Jagoda told a news conference, adding that there could be a slight improvement in October, but nothing dramatic.
Economists, who pay much closer attention to the adjusted unemployment data, were not expecting such a sharp rise in joblessness and began to question the speed of recovery.
"This is certainly a setback for hopes that the economy is gaining momentum," Deutsche Bank senior economist Rainer Veit told Reuters Financial Television.

The German economy rebounded to 1.2 percent year-on-year economic growth in the second quarter from 0.2 percent in the first quarter, but the government still forecasts growth of just 0.75 to one percent for the full year.
The weak unemployment data alone would not be enough to convince the Bundesbank to lower its securities repurchase rate, the central bank's key "repo", economists said.
But most economists agreed that the continued slump on the jobs front would cause the central bank to take a long, hard look at the economy and the state of recovery.
The rise in unemployment reflected uncertainty by companies about making new investments, said Barclays de Zoete Wedd economist Mathias Haffner.
"It looks like companies are still very reluctant to hire new people, possibly also because of the insecurity with relation to changes in labour legislation, for example in sick-pay," he said.
Asked whether the data showed that economic growth was faltering, Haffner said: "Other economic indicators do not point in that direction yet."

German exports have benefited recently from the weakening of the mark against major currencies, particularly the dollar and the Italian lira, but domestic demand has remained weak, another reason for uncertainty in industry.

Economist Shanda Persaud of San Paulo Bank in London warned that benefits to German manufacturers from the weaker mark could fade by year-end. This could present problems on the labour market if domestic demand remained weak as well.

In west Germany, adjusted unemployment rose 34,000 to 2.748 million. The rate rose to 9.3 percent from 9.1 percent. In east Germany, the number of unemployed rose 4,000 to 1.140 million, while the rate rose to 15.3 percent from 15.2 percent.
Labour office researcher Hanspeter Leikeb said he expects a small fall in employment in the German construction sector in the fourth quarter.

"From June to September we saw the positive effects in the construction sector of the recovery due to seasonal factors. But at the end of the year I expect we will see a fall," he said. Germany has seen clear jobs growth in service sector, which has been growing strongly, he added.
